_readme: THE PUBLISHED-CLAIMS REGISTER — [pipeline K-3] Private/requirements/ (was pipeline/08-compliance-legal.md, folded into the JSON spec 2026-08-15)
One row for every EMPHASISED claim in the visible text of the published legal pages in `pages` below, paired to
whatever in this tree makes it true — or, where nothing does, to the owner item that will.
🔴 WHAT MAKES THIS UNFAKEABLE, AND IT IS THE ONLY REASON THE FILE IS WORTH HAVING.
The domain is not this file. The domain is the set of <b>/<strong> spans in the visible text of
sites/nikatru/{privacy,terms,refund,shipping,delete-account}.html, extracted by tooling/ci/text-reductions.mjs.
shipping.html joined that set on 2026-09-09: /shipping is one of the four policy URLs a payment provider
collects, so leaving it outside the domain was a hole in the guard rather than a page that owed nothing.
The guard requires
the two sets to be EQUAL, both directions:
· a span with no row FAILS — you cannot publish a new emphasised promise without recording it;
· a row with no span FAILS — you cannot keep a row for a sentence the site no longer makes.
Neither side can be shrunk without editing a published document, which is a visible change a human
reviews. A register that listed only its own rows would be a list somebody trims when it is
inconvenient; this one cannot be.
⚠️ HONEST LIMITATION, AND THE GUARD'S HEADER SAYS THE SAME THING. Only rows typed `code` carry a
mechanical assertion. A `descriptive` row proves that somebody looked at the sentence and wrote it
down — nothing more. THIS FILE DOES NOT PROVE THE PAGES ARE TRUE. It proves that every emphasised
claim is accounted for, and that the specific claims we CAN check against code still hold.
Row types:
code        an assertion below runs against real files and can fail. This is the load-bearing kind.
provider    the claim names a third party; it must resolve to a row in provider-register.json.
descriptive the claim is a statement of intent, a defined term, or a commitment with no code
consequence (a refund window, a heading, the trading name). Paired, not proven.
known-gap   the claim is WRONG or contradicted today, and fixing it means editing published legal
copy — owner work. Carries an ownerItem and PRINTS on every run.
seller-by-rail  ⏱ 2026-09-26 (O-PRIVACY-OMITS-THE-INDIA-SELLER). NOT a span row: it carries `rail`, `pages` and
`note`, no `page` or `claim`. One per selling rail of tooling/channel-register.json `purchaseRails.rails`
(`none` aside). The rail resolves to its provider through provider-register.json `requiredWhen.rail`,

the provider's role gives `sellerIs`, and each listed page must say that seller in one

or
that names the provider. A rail with no row FAILS; zero rows, or a rail no provider resolves to, is
COVERAGE LOST.
Enforced by tooling/ci/assert-policy-claims.mjs. COVERAGE LOST if zero spans are extracted from any
page: an emphasis-stripping rewrite must be loud, not silently satisfying.
⚠️ `claim` IS THE NORMALISED SPAN TEXT (entities decoded, whitespace collapsed, curly quotes and
dashes folded onto ASCII — see html-text.mjs normaliseForMatch). It is compared to the page, not
typed from memory; if a row here does not match, the page is what is right.

claims.why: The name of the in-app control, in both trees that render one: tooling/bricks/app/__brick__/apps/{{app_id}}/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart builds a tile from l10n.deleteAccount, and apps/subscriptiontracker/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart ships the same control ([ADR 027]). The page used to hedge — "where an app shows a Delete account control" — precisely because apps/subscriptiontracker had none; the hedge is gone because the control landed. What keeps the sentence true is tooling/ci/assert-deletion-control.mjs, which quantifies over the brick AND every apps/* workspace member with NO exemptions and fails the build for any app that offers accounts without one; the `account-deletion-works` key in assert-stamp-properties.mjs covers the stamped half.
Where that control lives. Same screen file as above; the tile is built inside the settings screen and nowhere else.

claims.claim: the same email address and password no longer sign in anywhere
claims.why: The identity limb of services/platform/src/routes/account.ts: the Supabase admin user record is deleted LAST, and the route answers 502 rather than ok:true when that call fails. services/platform/test/auth.test.ts asserts on the request the route MADE, which is the one limb row counts cannot fake. The route answers 501 while SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY is unset (an owner action) — which is why section 1 keeps the email route as a first-class path rather than a fallback, and why the in-app control reports that refusal in the words "Nothing was deleted" instead of a generic failure ([ADR 027], packages/core/lib/src/auth/account_deletion.dart).

The two tables tooling/legal/data-inventory.json declares with erasure kind `pseudonymous`. The claim that follows is checkable and is checked there: neither table carries a user-shaped column, and the guard fails if one is ever added.

[ADR 020]: no anon_id -> user_id map may ever be written. services/platform/migrations/0002_analytics.sql keys both tables on anon_id, and tooling/ci/assert-data-inventory.mjs fails the `pseudonymous` declaration the day either table grows a `user_id` or *_user_id column.

claims.claim: Records of a payment we could not match to any account.
claims.why: `unclaimed_payments` (services/platform/migrations/0004_money_rail.sql section D). The sentence that follows it — the account link is removed, the record stays — is the `unlink` erasure kind, proven by services/platform/test/erasure-reach.test.ts, which asserts the row survives and the column is NULL.

claims.claim: What you created inside an app.
claims.why: The four `subscriptiontracker_db` tables tooling/legal/data-inventory.json declares with erasure kind `no-route`: services/platform's DELETE /v1/account reads PLATFORM_DB only, and services/subscriptiontracker-api has no account route. assert-data-inventory.mjs PRINTS that gap on every run. The paragraph exists because [ADR 027] shipped the in-app control WITHOUT closing that gap, and a section headed 'What is kept, and why' that omitted the user's own app content would be the omission the section exists to prevent. It comes down with the row, when a route reaches those tables.

Descriptive, and deliberately so: what a store does with its own records is outside this tree and nothing here can assert it. It is on the page because a reader who deletes an account and still sees a charge needs to know where to look.

claims.claim: Deleting an account is not reversible.
claims.why: True of the route by construction: the purges are DELETEs and the identity call is a DELETE, with no soft-delete column anywhere in services/platform/migrations/. There is nothing to restore from.
The trading name, defined here for the rest of the document. check-site-integrity.mjs separately asserts the LEGAL person behind it is named in visible text on this page.
A section heading introducing the category. The stores that hold it are enumerated in tooling/legal/data-inventory.json, which is where the checkable claim lives.
A section heading. Same as above — the inventory carries the store-level facts.

claims.claim: Usage statistics, only if you allow them

assert.why: 'only if you allow them' is a claim about a gate, and this is the gate: the analytics transport and the analytics sink both resolve to a no-op while consent is not granted. Deleting the check makes the page a lie, and this row goes red with it.

The page describes a stable per-install identifier and says plainly that records carrying it are pseudonymous rather than anonymous. `anon_id` is that identifier, and it is the column the events table is keyed on. If the server stopped carrying it the page would be over-disclosing rather than under-disclosing, which is still a page that does not describe the system.

claims.claim: We do not collect or store your IP address

assert.why: The strongest available reading of 'we do not collect or store your IP address' on the analytics path: the route that writes the events table never reads the header that carries it. The geo fields it does write come from `request.cf`, which Cloudflare derives at the edge. ⚠️ This asserts the header is not READ by this route — it is not a dataflow proof, and it says so rather than implying more reach than it has.

claims.why: A section heading. ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 087]: the list it describes moved from the KV namespace `nikatru-signups` to platform_db table `signups` (APAC). Its row in tooling/legal/data-inventory.json, `table:platform_db.signups`, carries the retention answer: `swept`, 400 days from the original signup time, deleted by the platform Worker's nightly retention sweep; the `rl:` counter the same paragraph describes stays in KV (`kv:nikatru-signups`) with a one-hour expiry. The sentences beneath the heading are held by the two code rows that follow.

claims.claim: email address and the time you signed up

assert.why: 'and nothing else' is the claim, and this is the whole record. The moment somebody adds a third field to that object literal this row goes red, which is exactly when the page stops being true. This is the most precise pairing in the file: one published sentence, one line of code.

A KEYED construction, not a digest: an unsalted sha256 of an IPv4 address is reversible by exhausting 2^32 values, so it would be the address wearing a hash and the page would be wrong. check-site-integrity.mjs enforces the same property from the code side; this row is what ties it to the published sentence.

claims.why: A section heading. The providers in the purchase path are enumerated in tooling/legal/provider-register.json.

claims.claim: do not collect or store your full card or bank details.

assert.why: No schema in any Worker may declare a column that holds a payment instrument. Walked rather than listed so a NEW migration file is covered the day it lands, and floored at the 5 migration files that exist today so a walk that stops finding them is COVERAGE LOST rather than a pass. ⚠️ A column-name blocklist is a tripwire, not a proof: it catches the obvious spelling of a card column, not a card number stuffed into a `notes` field.

claims.why: Two separate one-word emphases — 'We do NOT sell your personal information' (§1) and 'likewise NOT sent to a third-party analytics product' (§3). Both collapse to the same span text, so they share one row; the substantive claims they belong to are carried by the surrounding rows.

claims.claim: In an app from the Apple App Store or Google Play
claims.note: ⏱ 2026-09-26 · O-PRIVACY-OMITS-THE-INDIA-SELLER. Replaces the span 'Apple App Store, Google Play and Microsoft Store' of versions up to 2026-09-25, which named three stores as billers. Two of them bill: the apple-iap and play-billing rails of tooling/channel-register.json resolve to these two rows (requiredWhen mobileIapRail), both role store_billing, and the `seller-by-rail` rows for those rails make assert-policy-claims fail this page if the item stops saying the store bills the purchase.

claims.claim: On this website, in the Microsoft Store and in our direct downloads
claims.note: ⏱ 2026-09-26 · O-PRIVACY-OMITS-THE-INDIA-SELLER. The Paddle rail's reach, and the Microsoft Store's new place on the page: it moved OUT of the biller clause, because tooling/channel-register.json windows-store sells on `paddle` and this register's microsoft-store row says requiredWhen `never` — the old sentence called it a biller, which both registers deny. The `Paddle` and `merchant of record` spans in the same item carry the seller; the `seller-by-rail` row for paddle holds it there.

claims.why: ⏱ 2026-09-26 · O-PRIVACY-OMITS-THE-INDIA-SELLER. The region the third §4 item is about, emphasised as the lead of that item the way the other two lead with where you buy. It is the region code IN of tooling/channel-register.json `regionRails` (chrome-webstore, edge-addons, amo → razorpay; [ADR 094]). Nothing asserts the word itself; the razorpay `seller-by-rail` row asserts the seller statement it introduces.

⏱ 2026-09-26 · O-PRIVACY-OMITS-THE-INDIA-SELLER. The India seller, stated where it was missing until policy version 2026-09-26 ([ADR 076] §10, [ADR 094]). Not typed `code`: no file in this tree sells anything. What holds the sentence is the razorpay `seller-by-rail` row — its provider's role payment_gateway says sellerIs `nikatru`, so assert-policy-claims fails this page if no block names Razorpay with 'Nikatru is the seller'. The same span on refund.html is a known-gap only because the rail is not live and that page describes how a refund on it is issued; this page says in the same section that nothing is sold from the website today.

claims.note: ⏱ 2026-09-26 · O-PRIVACY-OMITS-THE-INDIA-SELLER. The India gateway, named on this page for the first time at policy version 2026-09-26 and disclosed as a processor acting on our behalf, never as the seller. provider-register.json razorpay `namedIn` now lists privacy.html, so §3(b) re-reads the page for it on every run.

Two spans on this page carry this text and BOTH are now true. They were not on version 2026-08-01: the second sentence said usage statistics AND crash reports both run on Cloudflare, and crash reports run on Oracle Cloud. The 2026-08-10 signature split that sentence so each system names its own host, which is what retired the `crash-reports-infrastructure` gap. The note is kept rather than deleted because the defect it records is the reason a per-span row cannot distinguish two identical spans — if a future edit re-merges the sentence, this row goes green on a page that is wrong again.

The ROLE, now stated beside the provider that fills it rather than instead of one. [ADR 004] locked Paddle and [ADR 039] D1 scoped it to every channel an app store does not bill itself; the `Paddle` span in the same sentence carries the name. The `merchant-of-record-unnamed` gap was retired by the 2026-08-10 signature.

The seller named, closing `merchant-of-record-unnamed`. terms.html and refund.html named Paddle on 2026-08-10 without a version bump because they carry no policy version; privacy.html could not, which is why this span waited for the signature and arrived with it. The register's `namedIn` for paddle now lists all three pages, so assert-policy-claims re-checks the disclosure against the page text on every run.

The IAP aggregator ([ADR 039] D5), disclosed as a PROCESSOR and never as a seller — the sentence says it 'processes that on our behalf and is never the seller', because a buyer contracts with the store or with Paddle, never with RevenueCat. Closes `iap-aggregator-unnamed`. It holds no live data today (every kind:store row in tooling/channel-register.json is served:false), which is exactly why the disclosure had to land before the first store purchase rather than after it.

The identity provider, wired by the cut-1 auth reversal (#280) and disclosed here. Closes `identity-provider-unnamed`. Nothing is stored under it today because no shipped app offers accounts — this is a disclosure that had to precede the first account, not one that was wrong.

⏱ 2026-09-25 · O-SIGN-IN-PROVIDERS-UNDISCLOSED. An OPTIONAL sign-in method, named in the sentence that also says what it shares (the email address and name on the account, as the user allows) and that the name can be changed in Settings. What makes it true in this tree: packages/auth_supabase/lib/src/auth_providers.dart `AuthProviders.configured` (apple: true), the email and password form every sign-in screen keeps beside it, and the Settings display-name edit (apps/subscriptiontracker/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart). The Name row in apps/subscriptiontracker/store/android-play/data-safety.json is the sworn half of the same sentence.

⏱ 2026-09-25 · O-GOOGLE-SIGN-IN-NOT-BUILT. BUILT AND OFF: `AuthProviders.configured` says google: false, so no app offers it yet, and the sentence opens 'Where an app offers them' for that reason. tooling/ci/assert-auth-callbacks.mjs refuses google: true while apple is false. Named before the switch on purpose, so the disclosure is in place before the button is. ⏱ 2026-09-26: ON. `AuthProviders.configured` says google: true, flipped with the live project in one window; the sentence's 'Where an app offers them' stays true.

🔴 THE FIFTH CORRECTION, AND THE ONLY ONE WITH NO GAP ROW BEHIND IT. The other four privacy.html omissions signed on 2026-08-10 were each carried as a `disclosureGaps` row that printed on every CI run; Resend was carried by nothing, because it was absent from tooling/legal/provider-register.json entirely — and every guard here quantifies over that register. It has delivered Supabase auth mail (and therefore held every user's email address) since auth mail went live under [ADR 029]. Found by inspection during the signature, not by a check. TRANSACTIONAL ONLY: the sentence names sign-in and account-verification messages and asserts no marketing channel, because ConsentPurpose.marketingEmail is collection-only with no sender and no list ([ADR 040] decision 5).

Where crash reports actually land. Closes `crash-reports-infrastructure`: the sentence used to cover usage statistics and crash reports with one host and was wrong about the second. Split at the 2026-08-10 signature so each system names its own. tooling/legal/provider-register.json already declared `crash_report` against the crash sink, so the page was the only half of the pair that disagreed with the register. ⏱ CORRECTED IN THE 2026-09-05 POLICY MINT: this row said `Oracle Cloud` / `oracle-cloud` and the page said the same, and both had been wrong since 2026-09-02 — the GlitchTip instance moved to Box B (Hostinger) on that date, `tooling/ops/register.json` `_substrateHosts.glitchtip-heartbeat` already resolved to `hostinger`, and the published page went on naming the machine the service had left. A provider row is an identity, not a label: the sink row was renamed with the machine rather than relabelled, so the page, this row and the register name one provider again.

claims.claim: We do not use advertising networks or advertising SDKs, we do not sell or share data with data brokers or advertisers, and no Nikatru app carries third-party advertising.

assert.why: A package manifest can refute the THIRD-PARTY half of this sentence outright: an advertising or attribution SDK cannot enter this workspace without appearing as a dependency. Walked over every pubspec.yaml in the tree (floored at 10) so a new package is covered the day it is created. 🔴 THE WORD `third-party` IS LOAD-BEARING AND WAS ADDED DELIBERATELY ON 2026-08-10. The sentence used to read 'no Nikatru app carries advertising', and this walk could never have refuted THAT: Google Play's own ads declaration counts a house ad — 'a small ad banner, interstitial ad, ad wall, and/or widget' promoting our own apps — as advertising, keyed on FORMAT rather than on ownership or SDK presence (support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859455). A first-party promo surface adds no dependency, so the old claim would have gone false while this row stayed green — the exact silent-failure class this register exists to catch. The claim is now scoped to what the walk can actually see, and the first-party half is disclosed in §3 and asserted by the `first-party promotions`, `on your device` and `Offers and promotions` rows. ⚠️ A NAMED LIST IS STILL NOT EXHAUSTIVE; the standing trigger 'the day an ad SDK enters a pubspec' is the `global-privacy-control` row in tooling/legal/duty-matrix.json, and the trigger for the FORMAT question is `first-party-promotion-legal-basis` in the same file. The sentence, this row and apps/subscriptiontracker/store/android-play/ads-declaration.json remain pinned by exact string equality, so rewording any one without the others is a build failure.

'we show them ourselves, and no advertising network, ad exchange or advertising SDK is involved' is the half of §3 a dependency walk CAN refute, and it is the same walk the advertising row uses. Kept as its own row rather than folded into that one because the two sentences are in different sections and either could be edited without the other.

claims.claim: The legal basis we rely on.
claims.why: A lead-in, and a required disclosure: GDPR Art 13(1)(c) wants the purpose AND the basis. Descriptive because nothing in this tree can prove a legal basis is correctly chosen — that is a lawyer's judgement, and this register does not pretend otherwise (see its preamble).

The basis itself, GDPR Art 6(1)(f), with the SPECIFIC interest named in the same paragraph as Art 13(1)(d) requires. [research/44] V4 records why this is the basis rather than consent: Recital 47 treats direct marketing as capable of being a legitimate interest, and adding a consent gate would be legally unnecessary friction that wrongly implies the processing becomes unlawful when refused. The code agrees rather than merely not disagreeing: `ConsentPurpose.promo` in packages/core/lib/src/analytics/consent.dart carries `basis: ConsentBasis.legitimateInterest`, so `unknown` permits and only `denied` forbids. ⚠️ THE ROW IS `descriptive` AND THAT IS NOT A DODGE — the balancing test is the substance and no guard can perform it. What IS mechanical is the objection control, and it is asserted by the `Offers and promotions` row below.

claims.claim: What we use to decide what to show you.
claims.why: A lead-in to the targeting-inputs disclosure. The substantive claim under it — entitlement state only, decided on the device — is carried by the `on your device` row.

assert.why: 'the decision is made on your device' is the one sentence in §3 that a file can refute. [research/44] §4.3 specifies PromoGate as a PURE function over persisted counters — no UI, no config read, no I/O — so the decision must reach no network and emit no event. 🔴 THE FIRST LIMB IS THE SHARP ONE AND IT IS WHY THE PATTERN IS NOT JUST A LIST OF HTTP SPELLINGS: promo_gate.dart declares ZERO imports today (`library;` and nothing else), so `^\s*import\s` fires on ANY dependency arriving — a network client, an analytics rail, a storage rail, anything. A purity claim defended only by a blocklist of client names is refuted by the client whose name is not on the list; a purity claim defended by 'this file imports nothing' cannot be. The remaining limbs catch an impurity written inline without an import. Comments are stripped before matching, so the doc comment explaining that the gate touches no network does not trip it. NEGATIVE-TESTED 2026-08-10 by adding `import 'dart:io';` + `HttpClient().close();` to PromoGate.decide: assert-policy-claims went red with `dart analyze` clean, and restoring the file returned it to green.

claims.claim: Your right to object, and how to use it.
claims.why: GDPR Art 21(4): the objection right must be 'explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject and presented clearly and separately from any other information', at the latest at the time of the first communication. This lead-in plus the in-card control ([research/44] §7 rung 4, `PromoObjectionControl` inside `PromoSurface`) are the two halves of that; a Settings-only control would satisfy neither the 'separately' limb nor 'at the time of the first communication'.

assert.why: The page names a control and tells the reader where it is; this row is what makes that a promise rather than an intention. Modelled exactly on the 'Usage statistics can be withdrawn without contacting us.' row, which asserts `recordAnalyticsConsent\(` in the same screen file — delete the row from Settings and the claim goes red. 🔴 THE STRING IS ALSO THE SCREEN'S LABEL, AND THAT WAS NOT FREE: r4 shipped the l10n value as 'Promotional offers' while this signed sentence says 'Offers and promotions'. The page is the promise and the app string is not owner-gated, so the APP was moved to the page's words (apps/subscriptiontracker and the brick, en and ta) rather than the reverse — the page and the app must use one name for one thing, or a reader following the instruction hunts for a heading that is not there. NEGATIVE-TESTED 2026-08-10 by deleting the `recordPromoObjection` call from settings_screen.dart: assert-policy-claims went red with `dart analyze` clean, and restoring it returned it to green.

claims.why: The scope limit, and the sentence a store reviewer reads to decide whether the surface is an ad network. Descriptive today because v1 is SAME-APP ONLY ([ADR 040] decision 2) and there is no second app to promote — so nothing in the tree can yet be pointed at that would refute it. 🔴 IT BECOMES ASSERTABLE THE DAY A CROSS-APP SURFACE SHIPS ([research/44] §7 rung 6): the payload's app ids must all resolve to rows in catalog/apps.json, and that is the row to re-point this at rather than a new one.

claims.claim: Usage statistics can be withdrawn without contacting us.

assert.why: The withdrawal path in the one shipping app, in the screen the page tells the user to open. It is the same call the first-run prompt makes with `granted` flipped, so withdrawal appends a new consent artifact rather than editing the old one. Delete the row from Settings and this claim goes red — which is the point: the sentence promises a control, not an intention.

claims.why: Names the screen the user is told to open. The control on it is the subject of the withdrawal row above; this span is the signpost.
The label of the control, quoted so the page and the app use one name for one thing. The brick's own no-hardcoded-strings guard owns whether that label is localised.
The trading name. terms.html §preamble also names the sole proprietor, which check-site-integrity.mjs asserts.

assert.why: REPLACED THE `Razorpay` known-gap ROW. §4 previously told a buyer their website purchase was 'processed securely by Razorpay' — a company no code in this repository reaches, for a purchase the same site said does not happen, in a legal relationship a gateway is not ([ADR 004] locked a merchant of record; [ADR 039] D6 then confirmed Paddle serves Indian buyers too and that Razorpay is NOT the app rail). The page now names Paddle, so the pairing can be a real one: `MOR_VERIFIERS` is the merchant-of-record webhook registry, it is DATA rather than a URL shape (see the `_money` note in provider-register.json), and `paddleVerifier` is the only rail in it. Remove Paddle from that array and the page names a seller no money route can verify a webhook from — which is exactly when this row should go red. ⚠️ THIS ASSERTS THE RAIL IS REGISTERED, NOT THAT A SELLER ACCOUNT EXISTS: account state is private-SSoT material (OWNER_QUEUE A-1) and no in-tree guard can or should observe it.

claims.note: The ROLE, published beside the name for the first time. It is the operative disclosure rather than decoration: a merchant of record is the legal SELLER, so §4 now tells a buyer that Paddle — not Nikatru — is their counterparty, takes the payment and remits the sales tax. `tooling/legal/provider-register.json` roles.merchant_of_record is the same sentence in the register. Deliberately NOT a second `code` row: the terms.html `Paddle` row above already asserts the registry, and two rows asserting one fact inflates the apparent strength of this file (the honest-limitation rule in the preamble).

claims.why: A warranty disclaimer. Its scope and enforceability are a question for a lawyer, not for a guard, and this register does not pretend otherwise.

claims.claim: Nothing can be bought here today.
claims.why: A statement about the tree, and everything in the tree agrees with it: every kind:store channel in tooling/channel-register.json is served:false (only `web`, the site itself, is served), no merchant-of-record or gateway row in tooling/legal/provider-register.json carries a non-null `reachableAt`, and sites/nikatru/pricing.html loads no checkout script — its own source comment says so and the page's note repeats it in visible text. Descriptive rather than `code` because the honest assertion would be 'no checkout script is reachable from sites/', and no guard in this tree makes that claim today; a `code` row invented for it would be one regex standing in for a property nobody has defined.

claims.note: The India gateway named in §4. ⚠️ THE REGISTER IS BEHIND THIS PAGE AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT OF THE ROW: tooling/legal/provider-register.json carries razorpay at status `not-named-not-wired` with an EMPTY `namedIn`, and its notes record [ADR 039] D6 deciding that the India clause names Paddle and that Razorpay is not the app rail. The page now names it again, and there is still no Razorpay route, key or webhook anywhere in this repository (`reachableAt: null`). Nothing in this tree makes the sentence true; what it does today is disclose an intended domestic rail. The substantive half of that disclosure — that Nikatru, not Paddle, is the seller for those purchases — is carried as a `known-gap` on the refund.html row "Nikatru is the seller", which prints on every run until the register and the pages name one seller for India again. ⏱ CORRECTED 2026-09-22: the register is no longer behind this page in the way described above. [ADR 094] (LOCKED 2026-09-22) confirms Razorpay for every India surface, and the razorpay row now reads status `wired-not-live` with `namedIn` covering terms.html and refund.html, because `services/platform/src/lib/mor/razorpay.ts` exports a registered webhook verifier. The sentence 'no route, no key, no webhook' is therefore wrong about the webhook and still right about the route and the key — there is no Razorpay checkout and no `RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, so no rupee can be taken today. Everything before this ⏱ is the dated record of what was true until 2026-09-22 and is left verbatim.

claims.why: A commitment about billing behaviour, and nothing in this tree asserts it: no subscription is sold on any rail today (every kind:store channel in tooling/channel-register.json is served:false and no payment provider is reachable), so there is no renewal path to check the sentence against. It is here because it is the disclosure a store and a payment provider both require before the first sale, not because code backs it.

claims.claim: You may cancel at any time
claims.why: The cancellation promise. Descriptive for the same reason as the renewal row above — there is no subscription to cancel yet, and the three routes the sentence names (the store account, the Paddle receipt link, support@nikatru.com) are all outside this tree. The one cancellation-shaped control this repository DOES own is account deletion, which is asserted by tooling/ci/assert-deletion-control.mjs and is a different promise; nothing here should be read as proving this one.
The trading name.
